vectors.name: formats-yaml/temporals/native-date-resolves-with-no-schema
vectors.comment: YAML's core schema resolves a bare ISO-8601-looking scalar to date with no schema involved -- unlike JSON, which would leave this as a string until stage 2.

vectors.name: formats-yaml/sharp-edges/bare-time-resolves-to-sexagesimal-integer-not-a-time
vectors.comment: YAML's core schema has no standalone time type. A bare 12:00:00 resolves to the integer 43200 (twelve hours in seconds) -- YAML's own behavior, not an Omnist choice, and there is no read-side workaround once the parser has already produced an integer. Confirmed live against the reference implementation.

vectors.name: formats-yaml/sharp-edges/norway-problem-bare-on-key-resolves-to-boolean-and-is-rejected
vectors.comment: YAML 1.1's core schema resolves on/off/yes/no/true/false (in various cases) as booleans, not strings -- a bare `on:` key parses to the boolean true. Since a label MUST be a string, a reader MUST refuse to build a Document from a boolean-keyed mapping rather than silently coercing it. This is the exact failure mode that breaks an unquoted GitHub Actions `on:` trigger block. Confirmed live: the reference implementation reports this as a shape/label error, not a YAML-specific one -- quoting the key ("on":) is the only workaround, and there is none on the read side once resolution has already happened.

vectors.name: formats-yaml/encoding/doubled-leading-bom-is-rejected
vectors.comment: D-21: D-15 consumes exactly one leading U+FEFF and stops. The text that remains is parsed by this surface's own grammar, which admits no U+FEFF as content at offset zero, so the second mark is a syntax error. The position is 1:1 because it is computed on the text remaining after the strip. One of the two surfaces where this vector is red today. YAML 1.2 permits a leading BOM in its own right and the common libraries strip one before the grammar sees it -- layered under D-15's strip that is a second, undeclared strip, and two byte-different inputs build one Document with no diagnostic saying which byte was discarded. That is the outcome D-15 exists to prevent, so D-21 requires the reader to pre-check and reject. Measured: the reference accepts this input and returns the same Document as the single-BOM form (DIV-4).

vectors.name: formats-yaml/merge-key/sequence-merges-in-source-order

input.text:
base: &base
  region: eu-west-1
limits: &limits
  retries: 3
svc:
  <<: [*base, *limits]
  name: api

vectors.comment: The merge-key edge order rule, with no declared_max_* key of any kind so that no runner can skip it. Its twin in formats-yaml/alias-expansion.json carries declared_max_alias_expansion and is therefore skippable by any port that allowlists that key, which would have left the order rule with no vector exercising it at all. Merged entries come first, in sequence (source) order: base's, then limits', then svc's own -- region, retries, name. Red against the Python reference, which flattens a merge sequence in reverse (PyYAML 6.0.3 returns retries, region, name); the JavaScript yaml library 2.9.0 already returns source order. See DIV-4.

vectors.name: formats-yaml/merge-key/local-key-overrides-merged-key-in-its-place
vectors.comment: The collision half of the order rule: a key the referring mapping writes itself wins the value over the merged one, but keeps the merged key's position rather than moving to the end. So `e` is a = 99 then b = 2, not b then a. Measured identically in PyYAML 6.0.3 and yaml 2.9.0, and the Python reference already produces this -- green on arrival. Single-alias form, so the reversed-sequence artifact does not apply here.

vectors.name: formats-yaml/merge-key/earliest-alias-wins-a-collision-between-merged-keys
vectors.comment: Two aliases in one sequence supplying the same key: the earliest wins, so `r` carries the single edge a = 1, not a = 2 and not two a edges. One key means order cannot distinguish source from reverse flattening here, which is why this vector is green against the Python reference today while its sibling sequence-merges-in-source-order is red. Measured identically in PyYAML 6.0.3 and yaml 2.9.0.

vectors.name: formats-yaml/merge-key/sequence-collision-keeps-first-position-and-value-precedence
vectors.comment: Order and value precedence in one shape, and the shape that separates the two implementations. Under the rule: merged entries in sequence order give a (from p), b (from p, which is the earliest alias supplying it, so p's 5 wins over q's 2), then c (from q, at q's position); the referring mapping's own c = 99 then wins the value while keeping that position. Result a = 1, b = 5, c = 99 in that order. yaml 2.9.0 returns exactly this. PyYAML 6.0.3 returns the same three values in the order b, c, a -- the reversed-sequence artifact -- so the Python reference is red here. See DIV-4.

vectors.name: formats-yaml/merge-key/nested-merge-puts-the-grandparent-first
vectors.comment: A merge nests: `m` merges `g`, and `n` merges `m`, so `n` gets g's entries, then m's own, then n's own -- a, b, c. The merged-entries-first rule applies at each level, which is what puts the grandparent ahead of the parent. Every alias here is a single-alias merge, so the reversed-sequence artifact does not apply and the Python reference already produces this. Measured identically in PyYAML 6.0.3 and yaml 2.9.0.

vectors.name: formats-yaml/merge-key/repeated-alias-in-one-sequence-contributes-once
vectors.comment: The same anchor twice in one merge sequence contributes one copy, not two: the second occurrence supplies only keys the first already supplied, and the collision rule collapses each to a single edge at its first position. A Document is an ordered edge list and repeated labels are legal in it, so this is a real question rather than an obvious one -- `r` could have carried four edges. It carries two. Measured identically in PyYAML 6.0.3 and yaml 2.9.0, and the Python reference already produces this.
